reasons: An item without a model value opens an empty dialog with no message.
The starting light values are written in two places and must be kept in step.
The viewer is only a placeholder and does not load real object files.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and browser-only marker
sections.what: Marks the file as browser-only and brings in React, the 3D library, the orbit controls and the item type definitions.
sections.why: Likely reason: 3D drawing needs the browser, so the framework must not try to run this on the server. The code does not state this directly.
sections.watch_out: The path to the orbit controls file must match the installed version of the 3D library.

sections.name: buildObject
sections.title: Building the stand-in object
sections.what: Creates the shape for an item. A lattice is built from a three-by-three-by-three set of small cubes, with some removed, inside an outline box. The other shapes are a torus knot or an icosahedron, each with a solid body and thin outline lines.
sections.why: Likely reason: these are placeholder shapes that stand in for real objects until models are added. The code does not say this directly.
sections.watch_out: The lattice keeps every cube slot and shrinks the removed ones to almost nothing, so the number of parts stays fixed.

sections.name: VIEWS
sections.title: Preset camera positions
sections.what: Defines three named camera positions, Front, Side and Top, used by the view buttons.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The names suggest standard engineering views.
sections.watch_out: The Top view uses a tiny nudge on one axis. The reason is not stated, but it probably avoids the camera pointing exactly along the up direction.

sections.name: ModelViewer (part 1)
sections.title: Setting up the 3D scene
sections.what: Creates the renderer, camera, orbit controls, lights, grid and object, and stores a function for moving the key light. It also stores a function that starts a smooth camera move to a preset view. If the renderer cannot start, it records that WebGL is unavailable and shows a message.
sections.why: The fallback exists because some devices cannot run WebGL. The reason for the other setup choices is not stated.
sections.watch_out: This setup runs again whenever the item changes, so every change rebuilds the whole scene.

sections.name: ModelViewer (part 2)
sections.title: Animation loop, resizing and cleanup
sections.what: Keeps the canvas sized to its container, slowly spins the object unless reduced motion is on, and moves the camera during a preset view change. When the item changes or the viewer closes, it removes listeners and frees the geometry, materials and renderer.
sections.why: The cleanup releases graphics memory. The reason the spin is switched off for reduced motion is that it is an animation.
sections.watch_out: Every object created in the setup must be released in the cleanup. A missed object is a memory leak that grows each time the viewer opens.

sections.name: ModelViewer (part 3)
sections.title: Dialog layout and controls
sections.what: Renders the full-screen dialog with the item code and title, a return button, a drag hint, a placeholder note when relevant, the three view buttons, and the light strength and angle sliders.
sections.why: The sliders call the stored light function directly, so changing them does not rebuild the scene.
sections.watch_out: The starting light values, 1.6 and 45, are written both in the state and in the setup. If one changes without the other, the first frame will not match the sliders.

summary: A small interactive 3D viewer that shows one stand-in object, either a cube lattice, a torus knot or an icosahedron, with drag-to-rotate, zoom, preset camera views and light controls.
purpose: Lets a visitor inspect a simple 3D object linked to an Atlas item. It is a placeholder viewer, not a real model loader.
why: Likely reason: some Atlas items have no real 3D file yet, so simple shapes stand in for them. The code marks placeholder items with a label, which supports this, but the code does not say it directly.
how: 1. The buildObject function creates the shape named by the item. 2. The effect sets up a renderer, camera, orbit controls, two lights and a grid, then adds the shape. 3. An animation loop rotates the shape slowly unless reduced motion is on, and eases the camera toward any preset view. 4. Sliders call a stored function to change the key light's strength and angle without rebuilding the scene. 5. When the item changes or the viewer closes, the cleanup step stops the loop and frees graphics memory.
inputs: An Atlas item with a model field, a title and a code. A close callback. The three preset view names and the light sliders are fixed inside the file.
outputs: A full-screen dialog with a 3D canvas, three view buttons, a light strength slider and a light angle slider. It shows a message instead if WebGL is missing.
risks: If the cleanup misses something, graphics memory builds up each time the viewer opens. If the item has no model value, the effect exits without drawing anything, but the dialog still opens and shows an empty canvas. An unknown shape name falls back to the icosahedron.
debug: If the canvas is blank, check that the item has a model value and that the browser supports WebGL. If the sliders do nothing, check that the stored light function exists, which requires the effect to have run. If the page slows after several openings, check that the cleanup disposes everything created.
